propositions.statement: The objects of enquiry to the natural philosopher are principles and laws, not phenomena and insulated independent facts.
propositions.quote: it is principles, not phenomena,—laws, not insulated independent facts,—which are the objects of enquiry to the natural philosopher

propositions.statement: Truth is single and consistent with itself, so a principle may be as plainly elucidated by a simple fact as by an uncommon phenomenon.
propositions.quote: As truth is single, and consistent with itself, a principle may be as completely and as plainly elucidated by the most familiar and simple fact, as by the most imposing and uncommon phenomenon

propositions.statement: The fall of an apple may raise thoughts to the laws which govern the revolutions of the planets in their orbits.
propositions.quote: The fall of an apple to the ground may raise his thoughts to the laws which govern the revolutions of the planets in their orbits

propositions.statement: Nature operates with calm energetic regularity on an immense scale and with certainty in attaining her ends.
propositions.quote: the observation of the calm, energetic regularity of nature, the immense scale of her operations, and the certainty with which her ends are attained

propositions.statement: Food is necessary to the existence of man.
propositions.quote: First, That food is necessary to the existence of man.

propositions.statement: The passion between the sexes is necessary and will remain nearly in its present state.
propositions.quote: Secondly, That the passion between the sexes is necessary, and will remain nearly in its present state.

propositions.statement: The two laws of food and sexual passion appear to have been fixed laws of our nature ever since we have had knowledge of mankind.
propositions.quote: These two laws ever since we have had any knowledge of mankind, appear to have been fixed laws of our nature

propositions.statement: Since we have not hitherto seen any alteration in these laws, we have no right to conclude that they will ever cease to be what they now are.
propositions.quote: as we have not hitherto seen any alteration in them, we have no right to conclude that they will ever cease to be what they now are

propositions.statement: The Being who first arranged the system of the universe still executes all its various operations according to fixed laws for the advantage of his creatures.
propositions.quote: that Being who first arranged the system of the universe; and for the advantage of his creatures, still executes, according to fixed laws, all its various operations

propositions.statement: Population, when unchecked, increases in a geometrical ratio, while subsistence increases only in an arithmetical ratio.
propositions.quote: Population, when unchecked, increases in a geometrical ratio. Subsistence increases only in an arithmetical ratio.

propositions.statement: The power of population is indefinitely greater than the power in the earth to produce subsistence for man.
propositions.quote: the power of population is indefinitely greater than the power in the earth to produce subsistence for man.

propositions.statement: By the law of our nature which makes food necessary to the life of man, the effects of the two unequal powers must be kept equal.
propositions.quote: By that law of our nature which makes food necessary to the life of man, the effects of these two unequal powers must be kept equal.

propositions.statement: There is a strong and constantly operating check on population from the difficulty of subsistence.
propositions.quote: This implies a strong and constantly operating check on population from the difficulty of subsistence.

propositions.statement: Through the animal and vegetable kingdoms, nature has scattered the seeds of life abroad with the most profuse and liberal hand.
propositions.quote: Through the animal and vegetable kingdoms, nature has scattered the seeds of life abroad with the most profuse and liberal hand.

propositions.statement: Nature has been comparatively sparing in the room and the nourishment necessary to rear the seeds of life.
propositions.quote: She has been comparatively sparing in the room, and the nourishment necessary to rear them.

propositions.statement: The germs of existence contained in this spot of earth, with ample food and ample room, would fill millions of worlds in the course of a few thousand years.
propositions.quote: The germs of existence contained in this spot of earth, with ample food, and ample room to expand in, would fill millions of worlds in the course of a few thousand years.

propositions.statement: Necessity, an imperious all-pervading law of nature, restrains the germs of existence within the prescribed bounds.
propositions.quote: Necessity, that imperious all pervading law of nature, restrains them within the prescribed bounds.

propositions.statement: The race of plants, the race of animals, and the race of man are distinct races all subject to the great restrictive law.
propositions.quote: The race of plants and the race of animals shrink under this great restrictive law. And the race of man cannot, by any efforts of reason, escape from it.

propositions.statement: The race of man cannot, by any efforts of reason, escape from the great restrictive law of necessity.
propositions.quote: the race of man cannot, by any efforts of reason, escape from it

propositions.statement: Among plants and animals the effects of the restrictive law are waste of seed, sickness, and premature death.
propositions.quote: Among plants and animals its effects are waste of seed, sickness, and premature death.

propositions.statement: Among mankind the effects of the restrictive law are misery and vice, of which misery is an absolutely necessary consequence.
propositions.quote: Among mankind, misery and vice. The former, misery, is an absolutely necessary consequence of it.

propositions.statement: Vice is a highly probable consequence of the restrictive law but ought not, perhaps, to be called an absolutely necessary consequence.
propositions.quote: Vice is a highly probable consequence, and we therefore see it abundantly prevail; but it ought not, perhaps, to be called an absolutely necessary consequence

propositions.statement: Man cannot escape from the weight of the population law, which pervades all animated nature.
propositions.quote: I see no way by which man can escape from the weight of this law which pervades all animated nature.

propositions.statement: No fancied equality and no agrarian regulations, in their utmost extent, could remove the pressure of the population law even for a single century.
propositions.quote: No fancied equality, no agrarian regulations in their utmost extent, could remove the pressure of it even for a single century.

propositions.statement: The passion between the sexes appears to exist in as much force at present as it did two thousand or four thousand years ago.
propositions.quote: It appears to exist in as much force at present as it did two thousand or four thousand years ago.

propositions.statement: There are individual exceptions to the passion between the sexes now as there always have been, but they do not increase in number.
propositions.quote: There are individual exceptions now as there always have been. But, as these exceptions do not appear to increase in number

propositions.statement: It is an acknowledged truth in philosophy that a just theory will always be confirmed by experiment.
propositions.quote: It is an acknowledged truth in philosophy, that a just theory will always be confirmed by experiment.

propositions.statement: Experience is the true source and foundation of all knowledge and invariably confirms the truth of the argument.
propositions.quote: experience, the true source and foundation of all knowledge, invariably confirms its truth

propositions.statement: Suppositions whose probable realization cannot be inferred upon any just philosophical grounds must be put out of the argument.
propositions.quote: all suppositions, the probable realization of which cannot be inferred upon any just philosophical grounds

propositions.statement: The best arguments for the perfectibility of man are drawn from the great progress he has already made from the savage state, and the difficulty of saying where he is to stop.
propositions.quote: the best arguments for the perfectibility of man, are drawn from a contemplation of the great progress that he has already made from the savage state, and the difficulty of saying where he is to stop

propositions.statement: The race of plants and the race of animals shrink under the great restrictive law of necessity.
propositions.quote: The race of plants and the race of animals shrink under this great restrictive law.

propositions.statement: Every species has come into existence coincident in space and time with a pre-existing closely allied species.
propositions.quote: Every species has come into existence coincident both in space and time with a pre-existing closely allied species.

propositions.statement: Each species has had for its immediate antitype a closely allied species existing at the time of its origin.
propositions.quote: each one having had for its immediate antitype a closely allied species existing at the time of its origin

propositions.statement: No group or species has come into existence twice.
propositions.quote: no group or species has come into existence twice

propositions.statement: The complete renewal of the forms of life has occurred several times.
propositions.quote: This complete renewal of the forms of life also appears to have occurred several times

propositions.statement: The present organic world is derived by a natural process of gradual extinction and creation of species.
propositions.quote: the present condition of the organic world is clearly derived by a natural process of gradual extinction and creation of species

propositions.statement: The surface of the earth has undergone successive changes over an immense but unknown period.
propositions.quote: during an immense, but unknown period, the surface of the earth has undergone successive changes

propositions.statement: When multiple species share a common antitype, the series of affinities is compound and represented by a forked or many-branched line.
propositions.quote: the series of affinities will be compound, and can only be represented by a forked or many-branched line

propositions.statement: A country's peculiar species, genera, and families are the necessary result of long isolation permitting many series of species to form.
propositions.quote: A country having species, genera, and whole families peculiar to it, will be the necessary result of its having been isolated for a long period

propositions.statement: Most closely allied species are found in the same or closely adjoining localities, so affinity sequence is also geographical.
propositions.quote: the most closely allied species are found in the same locality or in closely adjoing localities; and that therefore the natural sequence of the species by affinity is also geographical

propositions.statement: Similar climates separated by sea or mountains often have closely allied representative families, genera, and species peculiar to each.
propositions.quote: In countries of a similar climate, but separated by a wide sea of lofty mountains, the families, genera and species of the one are often represented by closely allied families, genera and species peculiar to the other

propositions.statement: The distribution of the organic world in time is very similar to its present distribution in space.
propositions.quote: The distribution of the organic world in time is very similar to its present distribution in space

propositions.statement: Species and genera of the same geological time are more closely allied than those separated in time.
propositions.quote: Species of one genus, or genera of one family occurring in the same geological time are more closely allied than those separated in time

propositions.statement: Geological changes must occasionally have modified external conditions enough to render the existence of certain species impossible.
propositions.quote: Geological changes, however gradual, must occasionally have modified external conditions to such an extent as to have rendered the existence of certain species impossible

propositions.statement: Extinction is usually a gradual dying-out but may sometimes be sudden for species of limited range.
propositions.quote: The extinction would in most cases be affected by a gradual dying-out, but in some instances there might have been a sudden destruction of a species of limited range

propositions.statement: Rudimentary organs really do exist and in most cases have no special function in the animal economy.
propositions.quote: That these really do exist, and in most cases have no special function in the animal æconomy, is admitted by the first authorities in comparative anatomy

propositions.statement: The great law is that every change shall be gradual, so no new creature is formed widely differing from anything before existing.
propositions.quote: the great law which has regulated the peopling of the earth with animal and vegetable life is, that every change shall be gradual; that no new creature shall be formed widely differing from anything before existing

propositions.statement: Our knowledge of the whole series of former inhabitants of the earth is necessarily most imperfect and fragmentary.
propositions.quote: our knowledge of the whole series of the former inhabitants of the earth is necessarily most imperfect and fragmentary

propositions.statement: Whole formations recording vast geological periods are entirely buried beneath the ocean and beyond our reach.
propositions.quote: whole formations containing the records of vast geological periods are: entirely buried beneath the ocean, and for ever beyond our reach

propositions.statement: The hypothesis is in reality only one of gradual change rather than essentially a theory of progression.
propositions.quote: though it may appear to some readers essentially a theory of progression, it is in reality only one of gradual change

propositions.statement: No geologically very recent island possesses generic or family groups or many species peculiar to itself.
propositions.quote: no example is known of an island which can be proved geologically to be of very recent origin (late in the Tertiary, for instance), and yet possesses generic or family groups, or even many species peculiar to itself

propositions.statement: The Galapagos were first peopled by winds and currents at a period remote enough for original species to die out and modified prototypes to remain.
propositions.quote: They must have been first peopled, like other newly-formed islands, by the action of winds and currents, and at a period sufficiently remote to have had the original species die out, and the modified prototypes only remain

propositions.statement: A long period of quiescence or stability in physical conditions is most favourable to the greatest abundance and variety of organic life.
propositions.quote: a long period of quiescence or stability in the physical conditions of a district would be most favourable to the existence of organic life in the greatest abundance

propositions.statement: Going back along parallel or divergent series toward the common antitype, an analogy between two groups becomes an affinity.
propositions.quote: as we go back along the parallel or divergent series, towards the common antitype, the analogy which existed between the two groups becomes an affinity

propositions.statement: The hypothesis expects facts alone to be brought to disprove it, not a priori arguments against its probability.
propositions.quote: he expects facts alone to be brought to disprove it; not a à-priori arguments against its probabiliy

propositions.statement: In widely distributed genera, well-marked groups of species are peculiar to each geographical district.
propositions.quote: in widely distributed genera, well-marked groups of species are peculiar to each geographical district

propositions.statement: The great gaps between fishes, reptiles, birds and mammals would be softened by intermediate groups if all extinct forms were seen.
propositions.quote: The great gaps that exist between fishes, reptiles, birds and mammals would then, no doubt, be softened down by intermediate groups

propositions.statement: The natural series of affinities represents the order in which the several species came into existence.
propositions.quote: it follows that the natural series of affinities will also represent the order in which the several species came into existence

propositions.statement: When higher groups have become nearly extinct, lower forms that have better resisted modified conditions serve as antitypes on which to found the new races.
propositions.quote: whenever any of the higher groups have become nearly or quite extinct, the lower forms which have better resisted the modified physical conditions have served as the antitypes on which to found the new races
